title: Sita
hook: Rama tells Sita to stay home while he goes into exile, and she argues, and wins

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sita: a girl rising out of the furrow as King Janaka plowed, her name the line the plow cuts.

I will walk ahead of you. That, in paraphrase, is Sita's answer when Rama comes to tell her he's been sent into the forest, and that she should stay behind. The crown he was promised has been taken away. He's leaving soon. He has a careful speech ready about how she should live in Ayodhya while he's gone: honor his parents, don't praise him in front of the new heir. Sita doesn't take the speech. She takes the floor. Today: the argument in Valmiki's second book, where Sita's own words decide where she goes.
screen: `I WILL WALK AHEAD OF YOU.` → `A CAREFUL SPEECH, REFUSED.` → `SITA'S OWN WORDS DECIDE.`

segments.voice: She starts with a reason. A father, a mother, a brother, a son, she says, each lives by their own lot. A wife shares her husband's. If he is sent to the forest, so is she. Then she gets practical. I'll go first, and tread down the thorns and the sharp grass on the path. The forest with you is better to me than any palace without you. Rama tries again. He describes the forest honestly: wild animals, cold, hunger, sleeping on the ground. It's no place for you, he says. And here the text lets Sita get angry. In paraphrase: what was my father thinking, she asks, when he took you as a son-in-law? Did he think you were a man, when you're a woman in a man's form? It's a sharp line, and Valmiki keeps it. Then she weeps, and holds him, and Rama gives way. Come, he says. The Sita of this chapter is not quiet. She argues from duty, from love and from plain stubbornness, and she wins. Some readers hear devotion here first: a wife who will not be parted from her husband. Others hear a woman choosing her own road against the man trying to choose it for her. The text holds both, and gives her the words either way. The thorns she promises to tread down are hers to tread.
screen: `A WIFE SHARES HER HUSBAND'S LOT` · `I'LL TREAD DOWN THE THORNS` · `A WOMAN IN A MAN'S FORM?` · `DEVOTION, AND HER OWN ROAD`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one road ahead of you, a hard conversation, a move, a long week, and let someone you love come to mind alongside it. Ask quietly whether there's a thorn on that path you could tread down first, for them, and don't plan it; just breathe with whatever shows itself. If you pray, you can hold that person before God.
Sita. In Valmiki's second book, she refuses to stay behind, argues with Rama, and walks into exile at his side. Today's word.
Your line: Sita. The forest with him, over any palace without him. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sita's choice to follow Rama into exile is retold in Ramayana recitations and Ram Lila performances, and Hindu teachers read it both as a model of devotion and as a scene of her own strong will.

notes: Sarga numbers follow the vulgate numbering (Ayodhya 26–30); the critical edition numbers differ (roughly 2.23–27). Please confirm.

Ayodhya 30.3: confirm the paraphrase of Sita's rebuke (that Janaka, in choosing Rama, took a woman in a man's form for a man). It is a sensitive line; the lesson treats it respectfully and says Valmiki keeps it.
Ayodhya 27: confirm 'father, mother, brother, son each enjoy their own lot; a wife shares her husband's' and the thorns and kusha grass image.
'Don't praise him in front of the new heir' (Bharata) is from Rama's instructions in Ayodhya 26; confirm.
